PRIVATE REFLECTION: The case is a 64 y/o para 4 gravida 1 woman, BMI 39, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, OSA, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, levothyroxine, alcohol 1-2/week, smoking 2-3 cigs/d x15 y, prior cardiac cath negative. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Referral to dermatology and plastic surgery group practice.

Round 0-1 background: initial split malignant intertrigo vs hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa; allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis dismissed. Round 1 settled at ~5/9 for HS after reinterpretation of bullae as fluctuant abscesses and emphasis on apocrine risk profile, vs 4/9 for malignant intertrigo emphasizing true bullae, late age, active breast malignancy/immunosuppression and paraneoplastic intertriginous bullous eruption.

Round 2 public positions:
HS/acne inversa camp – Colleagues 1,10,2,7: apocrine triad axilla-inframammary-inguinal with simultaneous involvement is classic HS; large tense fluctuant lesions in axillae, erythematous inflammatory plaques inframammary, purulent nodules/draining abscesses inguinal = Hurley II-III nodulo-abscess disease with secondary bacterial colonisation. “Large bullae” read as clinical shorthand for tense fluctuant HS abscesses that rupture with purulent drainage, sinus formation and inflammatory plaques, not primary vesiculobullous change. Host phenotype is textbook HS severity: BMI 39, active smoking 2-3/d x15 y, T2DM, dyslipidemia, OSA/metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are strongest modifiable drivers of HS; metabolic comorbidities over-represented in Hurley II-III. Cyclophosphamide and diabetes amplify secondary infection/delayed healing, not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome. Late first presentation at 64 is compatible with long-standing undiagnosed disease worsened by cumulative metabolic/smoking burden; dermatology/plastic surgery referral fits drainage/debulking need. Malignant intertrigo is a mimic but classically more unilateral infiltrated weeping eczematous plaque related to primary, not recurrent purulent nodulo-abscesses across three synchronous apocrine sites.

Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum camp – Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9: distribution is apocrine but morphology is vesiculobullous/erosive-purulent rather than follicular nodulo-abscess → sinus → rope-like scar sequence. Explicit description is large true flaccid bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions: intensely erythematous oedematous macerated plaques with vesiculobullous change, fissuring, crusting and secondary purulent exudate. True primary flaccid bullae are not a feature of HS; HS “bullae” are fluctuant abscess cavities. Host context is aggressive intertrigo phenotype: 64 y, BMI 39, T2DM, current smoking, OSA, peripheral artery disease, active cytotoxic therapy with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma – breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung – and amplified by obesity, diabetes, chronic smoking and chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression. Presents with painful erythema, edema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and flaccid bullae in moist folds with secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth, frequently misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo, friction intertrigo or HS. New-onset bullous erosive intertrigo at 64 with active breast carcinoma on cyclophosphamide is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Purulent component explained by secondary infection in immunosuppressed diabetic host.

Disagreements persisting: nature of “large bullae” – true primary vesiculobullous change favoring malignant intertrigo/paraneoplastic erosive disease vs tense fluctuant HS abscesses mislabelled as bullae; onset age and malignancy context – 64 + ductal carcinoma + cyclophosphamide favors paraneoplastic intertrigo neoplasticum vs accumulation of obesity/smoking/metabolic risk favoring long-standing undiagnosed HS now presenting; morphologic emphasis – bullous erosive intertrigo with secondary infection in immunocompromised host vs chronic follicular occlusive disease with sinus formation.

Remaining uncertainties: need histopathology/immunofluorescence to distinguish true bullae/autoimmune paraneoplastic process vs abscess; distinction between malignant intertrigo as severe secondary infected intertrigo in obese diabetic immunosuppressed host vs intertrigo neoplasticum/carcinoma erysipeloides/cutaneous metastasis; para 4 gravida 1 notation flagged inconsistent earlier; option C is spelled Hidradenitis Supportiva, typographic error for suppurativa.

Current vote after round 2 is 6 for malignant intertrigo, 4 for HS. I still find the explicit description of large true bullae in axillae in a 64 y/o immunosuppressed patient with ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide more specific for malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum with secondary infection, although HS remains a compelling and frequently confused differential given identical anatomic distribution and strong metabolic/smoking risk profile. The decisive point remains histologic confirmation of bullae vs fluctuant abscess and work-up for active/recurrent breast disease.

reflection_text.6:
The case remains a 64 y/o woman, para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, OSA, type 2 DM, hypothyroidism; meds clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, levothyroxine; smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, 1-2 alcohol/week; cardiac cath negative. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions – three apocrine-bearing intertriginous zones with mixed bullous/erosive/suppurative morphology.

Deliberation round 2 remains split ~4 HS vs 6 malignant intertrigo. Option C is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva = typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa.

Pro-HS arguments now reiterated:
* Anatomical classic apocrine triad axilla-inframammary-inguinal with Hurley II-III nodulo-abscess disease; “large bullae” read as clinical shorthand for tense fluctuant HS abscess cavities that rupture with purulent drainage, sinus formation and inflammatory plaques.
* Host phenotype textbook HS severity drivers: BMI 39 obesity with friction/maceration, active smoking, T2DM, OSA/dyslipidemia/metabolic syndrome. Cyclophosphamide and diabetes amplify secondary bacterial colonisation and delayed healing, not create primary bullous disease.
* Late onset at 64 can occur with cumulative risk; chronic relapsing course fits dermatology/plastic surgery referral for drainage/debulking.
* Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum typically unilateral/infiltrated weeping erythematous-oedematous plaque with fissuring/crusting/ulceration, not recurrent painful purulent nodulo-abscesses with sinus across three synchronous sites.

Pro-Malignant Intertrigo arguments now reiterated:
* Morphology is true vesiculobullous/erosive intertrigo: large true flaccid bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal region. True primary bullae are not a feature of HS; HS gives follicular nodules → fluctuant abscess → sinus tracts → rope-like scarring, double comedones.
* Paraneoplastic/intertrigo neoplasticum phenotype linked to internal adenocarcinoma, classically breast/gastric/pancreatic/lung. Patient has known ductal carcinoma on cytotoxic immunosuppression, age 64, obesity, DM, smoking, immunosuppression – high risk for severe infected intertrigo/malignant intertrigo.
* New onset bullous erosive intertriginous disease at 64 with active breast cancer on cyclophosphamide is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade.
* Malignant intertrigo is frequently misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo, friction intertrigo or HS; purulent component explained by secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth in immunosuppressed diabetic host.

Key discrepancies unresolved:
* Are axillary lesions true primary bullae vs fluctuant abscesses miscalled bullae? Exact bullous morphology with pathology not available.
* Chronicity/duration not given; HS is chronic relapsing, malignant intertrigo can be rapidly progressive.
* Unilateral vs bilateral, presence/absence of double comedones, sinus tracts, rope-like scarring not specified.
* Para 4 gravida 1 notation noted as inconsistent previously.

Current understanding: both diagnoses fit apocrine triad and risk profile. The explicit mention of large true bullae in a 64 y/o with active breast carcinoma on cyclophosphamide favors a paraneoplastic intertriginous bullous process i.e. malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum with secondary infection. The overwhelming HS risk factor cluster and plausible clinical mislabeling of fluctuant abscesses as bullae keep HS a strong competing interpretation. Need clarification of lesion chronicity, exact bullous morphology/histology, evidence of sinus tracts/scarring vs true blistering erosions, and cancer recurrence work-up.
reflection_text.2:
The case is a 64 y/o obese BMI 39 woman, para 4 gravida 1, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, obstructive sleep apnea, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, light smoking 2-3 cigs/d x15y, on clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, levothyroxine. Dermatology/plastic surgery consult for inframammary lesions; exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions.

Core dispute remains whether the morphology is true primary vesiculobullous/erosive intertrigo or follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease described as “bullae”.

HS proponents in round 2: Colleagues 1,2,7,10 now argue the three-site apocrine distribution axillae-inframammary-inguinal is classic acne inversa/Hurley II-III. The “large bullae” are interpreted as tense fluctuant acute HS abscess cavities routinely documented as bullae/bulla-like in intertriginous zones, later rupturing with purulent drainage, sinus formation and inflammatory plaques. Host phenotype is textbook HS severity: BMI39 obesity with friction/maceration, active smoking, T2DM, dyslipidemia/OSA metabolic syndrome. Cyclophosphamide and diabetes amplify secondary infection/delayed healing, accounting for purulent component. Late onset at 64 is acknowledged atypical but late/worsening HS with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden is described. Malignant intertrigo is described as typically unilateral infiltrated weeping edematous plaque with fissuring/crusting/vesiculation, more neoplastic/eczematous, not recurrent painful purulent nodular abscesses with sinus tracts across three synchronous apocrine sites. Allergic/contact/atopic/psoriasis do not explain deep purulent nodules confined to apocrine folds.

Malignant intertrigo proponents in round 2: Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9 maintain morphology is bullous-erosive/weeping intertrigo rather than follicular nodulo-abscess. Explicit “large true bullae” in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions = intensely erythematous oedematous macerated plaques with vesiculobullous change, fissuring, crusting and secondary purulent exudate. True primary flaccid bullae are not a feature of HS. HS gives painful follicular nodules → fluctuant abscesses → sinus tracts → rope-like scarring with double comedones; “bullae” in HS are misnamed fluctuant abscesses, not primary blisters. Host context is severe infected intertrigo in oncologic/immunosuppressed/metabolically compromised elderly woman: age 64, active ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, obesity, T2DM, smoking, OSA/metabolic syndrome. Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma, breast/gastric/pancreatic/lung, amplified by obesity/diabetes/smoking/chemotherapy immunosuppression. New onset bullous erosive intertriginous disease at 64 with active breast malignancy on cytotoxic therapy is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Purulent component explained by secondary bacterial/Candida colonisation of severe erosive intertrigo in immunosuppressed diabetic host.

Retained nuances: Terminology confusion around malignant intertrigo as severe secondary infected intertrigo in obese diabetics vs paraneoplastic intertrigo neoplasticum vs metastatic carcinoma erysipeloides; some conflate with paraneoplastic pemphigus. Option C is misspelled Hidradenitis Supportiva for suppurativa. Para 4 gravida 1 noted as inconsistent by one colleague.

Round 2 shift: Colleague 1,2,10 flipped from A to C; Colleague 8 flipped from C to A. Current public split is ~6 A Malignant Intertrigo vs 4 C Hidradenitis Suppurativa, reversing the previous round majority.

Unresolved questions: Are axillary lesions true primary bullae/vesiculobullous change favoring paraneoplastic intertriginous bullous dermatosis or fluctuant HS abscesses clinically mislabelled as bullae? Is tri-site symmetric involvement and purulent nodularity more consistent with Hurley II-III HS with secondary bacterial infection exacerbated by cyclophosphamide, or with malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum in an immunosuppressed oncologic host? Age 64 with active ductal carcinoma and cyclophosphamide strongly favors malignancy-driven process, but classic HS risk burden obesity+smoking+T2DM+OSA is also strongly present.

Current belief is that the explicit description of large true bullae in axillae plus bullous-erosive plaque morphology in an active breast carcinoma patient on cyclophosphamide makes malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum the more parsimonious unifying diagnosis, while recognizing the HS risk factor cluster and the common clinical mislabeling of fluctuant HS abscesses as “bullae” makes hidradenitis suppurativa a major and plausible mimic that cannot be excluded without histopathology, microbiology, culture and evaluation for recurrent/metastatic breast disease.
reflection_text.4:
The case remains split between malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum A and hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa C, with a slight swing to A in round 2.

Case anchors unchanged: 64 y woman, para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, T2DM, dyslipidemia, OSA, peripheral artery disease, hypothyroidism, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, levothyroxine; smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d ×15 y, alcohol 1-2/week; prior negative cardiac cath. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions.

HS / acne inversa camp now Colleagues 1,2,10,7:
* Classic apocrine triad: axillae – inframammary – inguinal/groin with inflammatory nodules → fluctuant abscesses → purulent drainage and inflammatory plaques. “Large bullae” reinterpreted as tense fluctuant HS abscesses clinically mislabelled as bullae; true vesiculobullous change not required.
* Host phenotype textbook for severe HS: BMI 39 obesity with friction/maceration, active smoking, T2DM, dyslipidemia/OSA metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are strongest modifiable HS drivers; cyclophosphamide and diabetes explain prominent purulent component and delayed healing, not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome.
* Late onset at 64 acknowledged atypical but late/adult-onset HS with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden described. Dermatology/plastic surgery referral fits Hurley II-III drainage/debulking need.
* Malignant intertrigo dismissed as more unilateral, infiltrated weeping plaque often related to primary, not recurrent painful purulent nodulo-abscesses with sinus formation across three synchronous apocrine sites.

Malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum camp now Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9:
* True vesiculobullous/erosive morphology rather than follicular occlusive: large true bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions. True primary flaccid bullae are hallmark of intertrigo neoplasticum and not a feature of HS.
* High-risk host for severe intertrigo: elderly, obese, diabetic, current smoker, immunosuppressed by cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Malignant intertrigo is paraneoplastic intertriginous erosive/bullous eruption classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma breast/gastric/pancreatic/lung, with painful erythema, edema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and flaccid bullae with secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth; frequently misdiagnosed as HS/candidal intertrigo.
* Age 64 with active breast malignancy and cytotoxic therapy is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Primary large flaccid bullae not a feature of HS.
* Would prompt work-up for recurrent/metastatic breast carcinoma, carcinoma erysipeloides to skin folds.

Points carried forward:
* Whether “large bullae” are primary paraneoplastic blisters vs fluctuant abscesses described as bullae remains central disagreement; A-camp insists true bullae not HS; C-camp insists clinical misnaming explains wording.
* Definition of malignant intertrigo used variably: paraneoplastic cutaneous syndrome vs severe secondary infected intertrigo in high-risk host vs intertriginous metastatic carcinoma.
* Option C spelling error: Hidradenitis Supportiva = suppurativa.
* Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis unanimously rejected.

Unresolved discriminators: lesion duration/chronicity not given; unilateral vs bilateral; presence/absence of sinus tracts, rope-like scarring, double comedones; pain vs pruritus; active vs treated/recurrent ductal carcinoma; histopathology/immunofluorescence not provided.

Current belief: Both diagnoses remain plausible. The HS camp has strengthened its reframing of bullae as abscesses and leans on overwhelming metabolic/smoking risk profile and classic apocrine distribution. The malignant intertrigo camp leans on true bullous change, new onset at 64, active ductal carcinoma with cyclophosphamide immunosuppression, and classic paraneoplastic intertriginous bullous phenotype. Majority in round 2 leans A, but consensus not reached; decisive data would be chronicity, sinus tract/scar presence vs true blisters, and oncologic status.
reflection_text.9:
The case remains a tight A. Malignant Intertrigo vs C. Hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa, with round 2 now showing a slight A lead, ~5 A vs 4 C, after several flips from round 0: Colleagues 1 and 2 moved to C, Colleagues 3 and 4 moved to A.

Core clinical facts persist: 64 y/o woman, para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, type 2 DM, dyslipidemia, OSA, peripheral artery disease, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, plus clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, levothyroxine; smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, drinks 1-2 alc/wk. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Apocrine-bearing triad involvement undisputed.

Evidence for Hidradenitis suppurativa C, now emphasized by Colleagues 1,2,10,7:
* Classic acne inversa distribution axilla-inframammary-inguinal with nodulo-abscess spectrum; erythematous inflammatory plaques and purulent drainage.
* “Large bullae” reinterpreted as tense fluctuant HS abscesses clinically described as bullous; true primary vesiculobullous change not required.
* Textbook HS risk phenotype: BMI 39 obesity, active smoking, type 2 DM, metabolic syndrome/OSA/dyslipidemia. Smoking and obesity strongest modifiable drivers.
* Immunosuppression by cyclophosphamide and diabetes explain worsened secondary bacterial colonisation/delayed healing, not a primary paraneoplastic bullous syndrome.
* Late onset at 64 is atypical but late/worsening HS with cumulative metabolic/tobacco burden is described; referral to dermatology/plastic surgery fits Hurley II-III need for drainage/debulking.
* Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis do not produce deep purulent nodules/abscesses confined to apocrine folds.

Evidence for Malignant Intertrigo A, now emphasized by Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9:
* Intertriginous erosive-bullous dermatosis in moist apocrine flexures: true large bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques in inframammary folds, purulent/erosive lesions in inguinal region.
* High risk host for severe intertrigo: elderly obese diabetic smoker, immunosuppressed by cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is paraneoplastic with internal adenocarcinoma – breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung – presenting with intense erythema, edema, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and vesiculobullous change with secondary purulent exudate, often misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo or HS.
* True primary bullae are not a feature of HS; HS gives follicular nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts and rope-like scarring, usually onset 2nd-3rd decade. Onset at 64 with active malignancy and cytotoxic therapy makes de novo HS less parsimonious.
* Some frame malignant intertrigo as intertriginous metastatic carcinoma/carcinoma erysipeloides, especially breast primary in inframammary area.

Key unresolved / sources of disagreement:
* Morphology language: are “large bullae” true primary blisters of vesiculobullous paraneoplastic intertrigo, or fluctuant abscesses mislabelled as bullae? No histology, duration/course, presence of sinus tracts/scarring, double comedones, bilateral vs unilateral involvement provided.
* Significance of ductal carcinoma + cyclophosphamide: paraneoplastic/malignant intertrigo driver vs simple comorbidity burden plus immunosuppression worsening HS suppuration.
* Age of onset: classic HS 2nd-3rd decade vs malignant intertrigo described in elderly metabolically compromised hosts.
* Conceptual conflation noted: malignant intertrigo framed variably as paraneoplastic pemphigus/intertriginous autoimmune bullae vs carcinoma erysipeloides/cutaneous metastasis. Option C spelling “Supportiva” is typographic error for suppurativa, repeatedly noted.
* Para 4 gravida 1 inconsistency flagged as chart error, irrelevant.

Current synthesis: Both diagnoses explain apocrine triad and risk factors. Pro-HS camp argues bullae are abscesses, metabolic/tobacco risk profile is textbook HS, immunosuppression explains purulence. Pro-malignant intertrigo camp holds true bullae plus active breast malignancy/cyclophosphamide in 64 y/o favors erosive bullous paraneoplastic intertrigo and HS does not produce primary bullae. Decision hinges on confirmation of true vesiculobullous change vs fluctuant nodular abscesses, chronicity/sinus tracts/scarring, and histopathology/biopsy for malignant intertrigo vs follicular occlusion disease.
reflection_text.5:
The case remains a 64 y/o obese BMI 39 woman with T2DM, OSA, dyslipidemia, PAD, hypothyroidism, active smoking 2-3 cigs/d ×15y, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, levothyroxine. Exam described as large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Para 4 gravida 1 is inconsistent and likely a chart error.

Round 0 was 5 vs 5 A malignant intertrigo vs C hidradenitis suppurativa. Round 1 shifted toward C ~6 C vs 4 A with reinterpretation of “bullae” as tense fluctuant HS abscesses. Round 2 now 6 A vs 4 C, swing back toward malignant intertrigo.

Arguments for A. Malignant Intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum, advanced in Round 2 by Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9:
* Explicit morphology is true vesiculobullous-erosive intertrigo: large true flaccid bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring/crusting in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions. True primary bullae are not a HS feature.
* Paraneoplastic / severe infected intertrigo phenotype in elderly, obese, diabetic, immunosuppressed host with known ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide. Malignant intertrigo is described as painful erythema, edema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and vesiculobullous change with secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth, classically linked to adenocarcinoma breast/gastric/pancreatic/lung and amplified by obesity, diabetes, smoking and chemotherapy.
* Age 64 new onset bullous erosive intertrigo is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Symmetric tri-site bullous erosive disease is a classic misdiagnosis trap for malignant intertrigo vs candidal intertrigo/friction intertrigo/HS.
* No mention of double comedones, chronic sinus tracts, rope-like scarring; “bullae” wording is taken literally.

Arguments for C. Hidradenitis Suppurativa / acne inversa, advanced in Round 2 by Colleagues 1,2,10,7:
* Classic apocrine-bearing triad involvement: axillae, inframammary folds, inguinal regions with painful nodulo-abscesses, erythematous inflammatory plaques and purulent drainage/sinus formation.
* Host phenotype is essentially HS: BMI 39, active smoking, T2DM, dyslipidemia, OSA/metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are strongest modifiable drivers of HS severity.
* “Large bullae” are reinterpreted as deep fluctuant acute abscesses/tense inflammatory nodules routinely documented as bullae-like in intertriginous skin, which later rupture with purulent drainage, sinus formation and inflammatory plaques. That fits Hurley II-III nodulo-abscess disease with secondary bacterial colonization.
* Cyclophosphamide immunosuppression and diabetes amplify secondary infection and delayed healing in established HS, explaining purulent component. Referral to dermatology/plastic surgery fits chronic relapsing disease needing drainage/debridement. Late onset at 64 is plausible with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden; long-standing undiagnosed HS can present later.

Key disagreements / unresolved:
* Nature of axillary lesions remains central: true large flaccid bullae vs fluctuant abscesses mislabelled as bullae. No histology, duration, chronicity/relapsing course, unilateral vs bilateral, presence of double comedones/sinus tracts/scarring, pain vs pruritus provided.
* Definition of malignant intertrigo remains variable: paraneoplastic intertriginous erosive/vesiculobullous syndrome vs severe infected intertrigo of obesity/diabetes/immunosuppression. Some colleagues conflate with paraneoplastic pemphigus/intertriginous autoimmune bullous disease.
* Age of onset: HS classically 2nd-3rd decade but late-onset/worsening disease is reported. Paraneoplastic intertrigo fits malignancy + immunosuppression.
* Option spelling “Hidradenitis Supportiva” is a typographic error for suppurativa, repeatedly noted.

Current understanding is still split, with Round 2 strengthening the A position on literal bullous morphology and oncologic/immunosuppressed context, while C retains strong support from risk factor phenotype and clinical reinterpretation of fluctuant abscesses as “bullae”. Discriminating data still needed: lesion chronicity and relapsing course, true blister histology vs abscess cavity, presence/absence of sinus tracts/scarring/double comedones, unilateral vs bilateral involvement, and workup for breast cancer recurrence / carcinoma erysipeloides / extramammary Paget.
reflection_text.3:
The case is a 64 y/o woman, para 4 gravida 1 – chart inconsistency noted, BMI 39, peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, obstructive sleep apnea, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism. Meds clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, levothyroxine; smokes 2-3 cigarettes daily ×15 y, 1-2 alc/wk. Cardiac cath negative. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Dermatology/plastic surgery referral.

Competing interpretations remain malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum vs hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa, option C listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva – typographical error for suppurativa.

Arguments for malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum that are reinforced in round 2:
* Morphology is explicitly bullous-erosive/weeping intertrigo in apocrine flexures: large true bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions. Described as intensely erythematous oedematous macerated plaques with vesiculobullous change, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and secondary purulent exudate. True primary flaccid bullae are not a feature of HS.
* Host is high risk for aggressive infected intertrigo: age 64, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes, active smoking, OSA/metabolic syndrome, peripheral artery disease, immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Malignant intertrigo is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma – breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung – and amplified by obesity, diabetes, smoking and chemotherapy. New onset bullous rapidly progressive intertriginous disease at 64 with active breast malignancy and cytotoxic therapy is atypical for de novo HS, which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade.
* Frequently misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo, friction intertrigo or hidradenitis. No sinus tracts, rope-like scarring, double comedones described; the pattern is symmetric tri-site weeping erosive disease rather than the follicular nodulo-abscess → sinus → scar sequence.

Arguments for hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa that persist and are refined in round 2:
* Classic apocrine triad involvement: axillae, inframammary folds, inguinal region with simultaneous painful inflammatory lesions. “Large bullae” reinterpreted as acute tense fluctuant HS abscesses deep in intertriginous skin, routinely documented as bullous/bullae-like and then rupture with purulent drainage, sinus formation and inflammatory plaques. Erythematous inflammatory plaques in inframammary folds and purulent nodules in groin fit Hurley II-III nodulo-abscess disease with secondary bacterial colonisation.
* Risk factor phenotype is textbook HS: BMI 39, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, OSA/metabolic syndrome, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/day ×15 y. Obesity and smoking are strongest independent modifiable drivers of HS severity; metabolic comorbidities are over-represented. Cyclophosphamide and diabetes explain prominent purulent component and delayed healing, not a primary blistering paraneoplastic process. Late-onset/worsening HS with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden is accepted.
* Referral to dermatology/plastic surgery fits chronic relapsing course with need for drainage/debridement.

Round 2 colleague distribution: 1,10,2,7 now favor C Hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa with the bullae-as-fluctuant-abscess re-interpretation; 3,4,5,6,8,9 favor A Malignant Intertrigo emphasizing true bullae and paraneoplastic/immunosuppressed erosive intertrigo. Colleagues 1 and 2 switched from A in round 0 to C in round 2; colleague 10 remained C.

Points of disagreement / uncertainty carried forward:
* Central hinge remains morphology of “large bullae”: true vesiculobullous change vs fluctuant abscess described clinically as bullae.
* Whether malignant intertrigo is paraneoplastic metastatic intertrigo / carcinoma erysipeloides vs severe secondary infected intertrigo in immunosuppressed diabetic obese host.
* Age atypicality for de novo HS vs paraneoplastic onset.
* Chronicity, presence/absence of sinus tracts, double comedones, rope-like scarring not clarified in vignette.

Errors / corrections noted previously remain: Option C spelling Supportiva; para 4 gravida 1 inconsistency.

Other options uniformly rejected: allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis do not explain deep purulent nodules/abscesses confined to apocrine folds with this risk profile.

Current belief remains unsettled. The explicit description of large true bullae in axillae in a 64 y/o immunosuppressed patient with active ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide continues to favor malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum with secondary infection, while the classic apocrine triad distribution, strong obesity/smoking/metabolic risk profile and the plausible linguistic mislabeling of fluctuant HS abscesses as bullae keep hidradenitis suppurativa a compelling unifying alternative. Histopathology, chronicity details, presence of sinus tracts/scar vs frank blisters, and work-up for active/recurrent breast disease would be decisive.
reflection_text.7:
Round 2 complete. Correct answer remains A. Malignant Intertrigo. Public split is C 6 – A 4.

Current supporters:
Correct A: Colleague 3, Colleague 4, Colleague 6, Colleague 8.
Incorrect C: Colleague 1, Colleague 2, Colleague 5, Colleague 7, Colleague 9, Colleague 10.

reflection_text.1:
The case is a 64 y/o woman, para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, obstructive sleep apnea, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism. Meds clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, levothyroxine; drinks 1-2 alc/wk, smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d x15y. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Dermatology/plastic surgery consult.

Core anatomic overlap persists: all three classic apocrine sites are involved – axillae, inframammary folds, inguinal/groin. That is the classic HS/acne inversa triangle and also the classic distribution for intertrigo neoplasticum/malignant intertrigo.

Risk factor cluster is shared and strong for both interpretations: BMI 39 obesity with friction/maceration, active smoking 2-3 cigs/d x15y, type 2 DM, dyslipidemia, OSA/metabolic syndrome. These are the strongest modifiable HS drivers and also the classic predisposing milieu for severe infected/malignant intertrigo. Additional high-risk modifiers are cyclophosphamide immunosuppression for ductal carcinoma and age 64 with diabetes and PAD.

The central dispute in rounds 1-2 is the meaning of “large bullae in the axillary folds” and the expected morphology.

HS proponents, Colleagues 1,10,2,7 in round 2, retain and strengthen:
* The lesions are read as the classic HS nodulo-abscess spectrum: tense fluctuant deep abscess cavities in axillae routinely documented as “bullae/bullae-like”, erythematous inflammatory plaques inframammary, purulent nodules/draining abscesses inguinal. Hurley II-III with secondary bacterial colonisation.
* Host phenotype is textbook HS severity; cyclophosphamide and diabetes explain purulent component and delayed healing, not a primary blistering process.
* Late onset at 64 is countered by late/worsening HS with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden; dermatology/plastic surgery referral fits chronic drainage/debulking.

Malignant intertrigo proponents, Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8,9 in round 2, retain and strengthen:
* Morphology emphasized as true vesiculobullous/erosive rather than follicular: large true bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions. True primary flaccid bullae are not a feature of HS; in HS “bullae” are misnamed fluctuant abscesses.
* High-risk host for malignant/intertrigo neoplasticum: 64y, BMI 39, T2DM, current smoker, immunosuppressed by cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma, PAD, metabolic syndrome. Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma – breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung – and presents with painful erythema, edema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and flaccid bullae with secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth in moist folds; frequently misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo, friction intertrigo or HS.
* New onset bullous/erosive intertriginous disease at 64 with active breast carcinoma on cytotoxic therapy is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade; no sinus tracts/double comedones/rope-like scarring are described.
* Para 4 gravida 1 remains an inconsistent notation.

Terminology confusion persists: “Malignant intertrigo” is used both as severe infected intertrigo in obese/diabetic/immunosuppressed hosts and as paraneoplastic intertrigo neoplasticum/carcinoma erysipeloides to skin folds.

Unresolved questions remain:
* Are the axillary lesions true primary vesiculobullous bullae vs fluctuant abscesses described as bullae? Clinical wording drives diagnosis.
* Is the disease acute paraneoplastic/erosive bullous intertrigo vs chronic follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease with secondary infection?
* How to weigh age of onset vs classic HS risk factor burden vs active ductal carcinoma + cyclophosphamide immunosuppression.
* Need for histopathology/biopsy, cultures, bacterial and Candida studies, and work-up for recurrence/metastasis of breast carcinoma to discriminate.

Current synthesis: The apocrine triad and risk factor profile strongly fit HS/acne inversa, and bullae can be mislabelled fluctuant abscesses. However round 2 majority now favors A, emphasizing explicit description of large true bullae, age 64 new onset, active breast carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, and classic paraneoplastic bullous/erosive intertrigo description for malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum. Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis remain not explanatory. Option C is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for suppurativa.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Malignant Intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum

The anatomic distribution is the classic intertriginous apocrine triad – axillae, inframammary folds and inguino-crural folds – but the morphology described is vesiculobullous-erosive intertrigo with secondary infection rather than chronic follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease.

Large true bullae are explicitly described in the axillary folds with erythematous edematous plaques within the inframammary folds and purulent erosive lesions in the inguinal regions. True primary flaccid bullae with weeping maceration, fissuring and erosive purulent exudate are the hallmark of malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum and are not a feature of hidradenitis suppurativa. In HS the so-called “bullae” are tense fluctuant follicular abscess cavities that rupture with purulent drainage, sinus tract formation and rope-like scarring with double comedones. No sinus tracts, chronic scarring or double comedones are described, and the explicit wording large bullae plus erosive plaques favours primary vesiculobullous change.

The host is the malignant intertrigo phenotype: 64 y/o, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes mellitus, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, obstructive sleep apnea / metabolic syndrome with dyslipidemia and peripheral artery disease, and active oncologic immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. New onset bullous-erosive intertriginous disease at age 64 in a woman with known ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide is atypical for de novo hidradenitis suppurativa, which classically begins in the 2nd-3rd decade. Obesity, smoking and metabolic comorbidity are present and explain diagnostic overlap, but they do not generate primary large flaccid bullae. Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis do not explain tri-site purulent bullous intertriginous disease in this immunosuppressed oncologic host.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Hidradenitis Suppurativa / acne inversa

I agree with the pro-A colleagues that malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum is a real concern here and cannot be dismissed, given a 64 y/o with ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes and active smoking. That oncologic/immunosuppressed context is exactly why this case is confusing.

On close re-read of the exam description I think the morphology is best read as follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease with secondary suppuration rather than primary vesiculobullous intertrigo. Axillae with large fluctuant lesions, inframammary folds with erythematous inflammatory plaques, and inguinal regions with purulent nodules is the classic axilla-inframammary-groin apocrine triad of acne inversa. In practice those tense fluctuant HS abscesses in intertriginous skin are routinely documented as “large bullae” and then rupture with purulent drainage, maceration and secondary erosive plaques. That explains the wording in the note without requiring true primary flaccid bullae.

The host phenotype is essentially the HS phenotype. The synchronous painful purulent nodulo-abscess pattern across three apocrine sites with this risk factor cluster is more parsimonious for hidradenitis suppurativa with secondary infection exacerbated by immunosuppression, diabetes, obesity and smoking.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa

I want to engage directly with the concern raised by Colleagues 3, 4, 6 and 8 about the “large bullae” wording and the oncologic background, because that is where the case is being pulled toward malignant intertrigo.

The distribution remains the decisive anchor. Simultaneous, symmetric involvement of axillae, inframammary folds and inguinal regions with large tense lesions in the axillae, erythematous inflammatory plaques in the inframammary folds and purulent nodules in the groin is the classic apocrine triad of acne inversa. That is not the relatively unilateral, infiltrated weeping plaque most closely related to a breast primary that is classically described for intertrigo neoplasticum / malignant intertrigo. Three synchronous apocrine sites with nodulo-abscess morphology is Hurley II-III HS.

On the morphology point, I think we are reading “large bullae” too literally. In intertriginous exam notes, especially from a dermatology and plastic surgery group practice that deals with chronic draining disease, tense fluctuant acute abscess cavities are routinely documented as bullae or bulla-like. Once they rupture there is maceration, fissuring, crusting and purulent exudate, which is exactly how the inframammary erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring and the inguinal purulent erosive lesions are described. True primary flaccid vesiculobullous change is not a required feature of HS; deep painful follicular nodules → fluctuant abscesses → sinus formation with secondary bacterial colonisation is. The note describes purulent nodules, not ulcerated metastatic plaques with epidermal atrophy.

The host phenotype is textbook severe HS and it explains the severity of the current episode. BMI 39 with friction and maceration in moist folds, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/day x 15 years, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia and obstructive sleep apnea / metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are the strongest reproducible modifiable drivers of HS onset, severity and poor response, and metabolic comorbidity is over-represented in Hurley stage II-III disease. Cyclophosphamide immunosuppression and diabetes do not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome here; they are exactly what we expect to amplify secondary bacterial colonisation, delayed healing and more florid purulence in established HS.

Age 64 is late for classic onset and the ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide is absolutely a real concern and needs ongoing surveillance, but late-onset and adult-onset/worsening HS with cumulative obesity, smoking and metabolic burden is well described, and new onset bullous erosive intertrigo at this age would still require histologic demonstration of metastatic disease for malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum. Malignant intertrigo remains a diagnosis of exclusion that classically presents with confluent erythema, oedema, fissuring, crusting and weeping erosions, often more unilateral, and it is not characterised by recurrent painful purulent nodulo-abscesses with sinus formation across three apocrine sites.

Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis do not give deep purulent nodules/abscesses confined to apocrine folds with this risk factor cluster. The most parsimonious unifying diagnosis is hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa, Hurley II-III with secondary infection exacerbated by obesity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and cyclophosphamide immunosuppression, referred to dermatology/plastic surgery for drainage/debridement. The option is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa.

C. Hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa

I want to engage directly with the concern raised by Colleagues 3, 4, 6 and 8 about the “large bullae” wording and the oncologic background, because that is where the case is being pulled toward malignant intertrigo.

The distribution remains the decisive anchor. Simultaneous, symmetric involvement of axillae, inframammary folds and inguinal regions with large tense lesions in the axillae, erythematous inflammatory plaques in the inframammary folds and purulent nodules in the groin is the classic apocrine triad of acne inversa. That is not the relatively unilateral, infiltrated weeping plaque most closely related to a breast primary that is classically described for intertrigo neoplasticum / malignant intertrigo. Three synchronous apocrine sites with nodulo-abscess morphology is Hurley II-III HS.

On the morphology point, I think we are reading “large bullae” too literally. In intertriginous exam notes, especially from a dermatology and plastic surgery group practice that deals with chronic draining disease, tense fluctuant acute abscess cavities are routinely documented as bullae or bulla-like. Once they rupture there is maceration, fissuring, crusting and purulent exudate, which is exactly how the inframammary erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring and the inguinal purulent erosive lesions are described. True primary flaccid vesiculobullous change is not a required feature of HS; deep painful follicular nodules → fluctuant abscesses → sinus formation with secondary bacterial colonisation is. The note describes purulent nodules, not ulcerated metastatic plaques with epidermal atrophy.

The host phenotype is textbook severe HS and it explains the severity of the current episode. BMI 39 with friction and maceration in moist folds, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/day x 15 years, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia and obstructive sleep apnea / metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are the strongest reproducible modifiable drivers of HS onset, severity and poor response, and metabolic comorbidity is over-represented in Hurley stage II-III disease. Cyclophosphamide immunosuppression and diabetes do not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome here; they are exactly what we expect to amplify secondary bacterial colonisation, delayed healing and more florid purulence in established HS.

Age 64 is late for classic onset and the ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide is absolutely a real concern and needs ongoing surveillance, but late-onset and adult-onset/worsening HS with cumulative obesity, smoking and metabolic burden is well described, and new onset bullous erosive intertrigo at this age would still require histologic demonstration of metastatic disease for malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum. Malignant intertrigo remains a diagnosis of exclusion that classically presents with confluent erythema, oedema, fissuring, crusting and weeping erosions, often more unilateral, and it is not characterised by recurrent painful purulent nodulo-abscesses with sinus formation across three apocrine sites.

Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis do not give deep purulent nodules/abscesses confined to apocrine folds with this risk factor cluster. The most parsimonious unifying diagnosis is hidradenitis suppurativa / acne inversa, Hurley II-III with secondary infection exacerbated by obesity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and cyclophosphamide immunosuppression, referred to dermatology/plastic surgery for drainage/debridement. The option is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The case is a 64 y/o woman, para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, obstructive sleep apnea, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism; meds clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, levothyroxine; drinks 1-2 alc/wk, smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y; cardiac cath negative. Exam: large bullae in axillary folds, erythematous skin regions with plaques within inframammary folds, purulent nodules in inguinal regions. Dermatology/plastic surgery consult.

Core anatomic overlap remains the apocrine triad: axillae, inframammary folds, inguinal/groin. Both HS/acne inversa and malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum involve these sites.

Risk factor cluster is strong for both and shared: BMI 39 obesity with friction/maceration, active smoking, type 2 DM, dyslipidemia, OSA/metabolic syndrome, peripheral artery disease. These are classic HS drivers and also classic predisposing milieu for severe infected/malignant intertrigo. Additional high-risk modifiers are cyclophosphamide immunosuppression for ductal carcinoma, age 64, diabetes.

Central dispute persists about morphology wording:

Pro-A majority in round 3, Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9, argue:
* Exam explicitly describes large true bullae in axillae, erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in inframammary folds, purulent erosive lesions in inguinal regions. True primary flaccid bullae with weeping maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and secondary purulent exudate is hallmark of malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum and is not a feature of HS.
* In HS “bullae” are colloquially misnamed tense fluctuant follicular abscess cavities that rupture with purulent drainage, sinus tract formation and rope-like scarring with double comedones. No sinus tracts, chronic scarring or double comedones are described.
* Host is classic malignant intertrigo phenotype: 64 y, obesity, T2DM, active smoking, OSA/metabolic syndrome, active oncologic immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Intertrigo neoplasticum is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma – breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung – and amplified by obesity, diabetes, smoking, chemotherapy.
* New onset bullous-erosive intertriginous disease at 64 with active breast carcinoma on cytotoxic therapy is atypical for de novo HS which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Para 4 gravida 1 remains an inconsistent notation.
* Work up for active/recurrent breast disease, carcinoma erysipeloides to skin folds, secondary bacterial and Candida infection is indicated.

Pro-C minority, Colleagues 10 and 7, argue:
* Distribution is classic apocrine triad of acne inversa. In practice tense fluctuant HS abscesses in intertriginous skin are routinely documented as “large bullae/bulla-like” and then rupture with maceration, fissuring and purulent exudate, explaining the wording without requiring true primary flaccid bullae.
* Host phenotype is essentially HS: BMI 39, active smoking 2-3 cigs/d x15 y, T2DM, OSA/metabolic syndrome. Obesity and smoking are strongest reproducible drivers of HS severity. Cyclophosphamide and diabetes amplify secondary bacterial colonisation, delayed healing and chronic suppuration in established HS.
* Late onset at 64 is late but late-onset/worsening HS with cumulative metabolic/smoking burden is described; dermatology/plastic surgery referral fits chronic drainage/debulking rather than acute paraneoplastic eruption.
* True primary vesiculobullous change with large flaccid bullae is not a feature of HS, but large fluctuant abscesses described as bullae are.

Unresolved questions remain:
* Are the axillary lesions true primary vesiculobullous bullae vs fluctuant abscesses described as bullae? Clinical wording drives diagnosis.
* Is this acute paraneoplastic/erosive bullous intertrigo vs chronic follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease with secondary infection?
* How to weigh age of onset vs classic HS risk factor burden vs active ductal carcinoma + cyclophosphamide immunosuppression.
* Need histopathology/biopsy, cultures for bacterial and Candida, and work-up for recurrence/metastasis of breast carcinoma to discriminate.

Terminology confusion persists: “Malignant intertrigo” used both as severe infected intertrigo in obese/diabetic/immunosuppressed hosts and as paraneoplastic intertrigo neoplasticum/carcinoma erysipeloides to skin folds.

Current synthesis after round 3: 8/10 colleagues now favor A. Malignant Intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum, emphasizing explicit large true bullae, age 64 new onset, active breast carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, and classic paraneoplastic bullous/erosive intertrigo description. Option C is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, typographic error for suppurativa/acne inversa. Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis remain not explanatory.

reflection_text.5:

A. Malignant Intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum

The distribution is the classic apocrine intertriginous triad – axillae, inframammary folds and inguino-crural folds – but the morphology as written is primary intertriginous bullous-erosive disease with secondary infection, not chronic follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease with sinus tract formation and rope-like scarring.

Large true bullae are explicitly described in the axillary folds, with erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring in the inframammary folds and purulent erosive lesions in the inguinal regions. The host is the malignant intertrigo phenotype. 64 y/o, BMI 39 with friction maceration in moist folds, type 2 diabetes mellitus, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, obstructive sleep apnea / metabolic syndrome with dyslipidaemia and peripheral artery disease, and active oncologic immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis do not explain tri-site purulent bullous intertriginous disease in this immunosuppressed oncologic host. The anatomic distribution is the classic apocrine intertriginous triad – axillae, inframammary folds and inguino-crural folds – but the morphology as documented is primary intertriginous bullous-erosive disease with secondary infection rather than the chronic follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess → sinus tract → rope-like scar sequence of acne inversa.

Large true bullae are explicitly described in the axillary folds with erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring within the inframammary folds and purulent erosive lesions in the inguinal regions. That is painful erythema, oedema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and vesiculobullous change with secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth. True primary flaccid bullae with weeping maceration, fissuring and erosive purulent exudate are the hallmark of malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum and are not a feature of hidradenitis suppurativa. In HS the “bullous” appearance is a tense fluctuant deep follicular abscess cavity that is routinely mislabelled clinically, and the classic stigmata are painful double comedones, recurrent follicular nodules, sinus tract formation and rope-like scarring. No sinus tracts, chronic scarring or double comedones are described, and the wording large bullae plus erosive plaques favours primary vesiculobullous change.

The host is the malignant intertrigo phenotype: 64 y/o, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes mellitus, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, obstructive sleep apnea/metabolic syndrome with dyslipidemia and peripheral artery disease, and active oncologic immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide for ductal carcinoma. Intertrigo neoplasticum/malignant intertrigo is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma, particularly breast, gastric, pancreatic and lung, and is amplified by obesity, diabetes, chronic smoking and cytotoxic therapy. It presents with painful erythema, oedema, maceration, fissuring, crusting, ulceration and flaccid bullae in moist flexures with secondary bacterial and Candida overgrowth and is frequently misdiagnosed as candidal intertrigo, friction intertrigo or hidradenitis suppurativa.

New onset, truly bullous erosive intertriginous disease at age 64 in a woman with known ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide is atypical for de novo hidradenitis suppurativa, which classically begins in the 2nd-3rd decade. The obesity/smoking/T2DM/OSA cluster is present and explains diagnostic overlap and the prominent secondary purulent component from impaired neutrophil function and immunosuppression, but it does not generate primary large flaccid bullae.

Allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and psoriasis do not explain tri-site purulent bullous intertriginous disease in this immunosuppressed oncologic host. Work up for active/recurrent breast disease, carcinoma erysipeloides to skin folds, secondary bacterial and Candida infection and histology of the bullae is indicated rather than routine Hurley staging for HS. Option C is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa.

C. Hidradenitis Suppurativa / acne inversa

I want to acknowledge the oncologic point that colleagues 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 are raising, because it is a real safety concern here. A 64 y/o with active ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes, active smoking and metabolic syndrome is exactly the host in whom we must keep malignant intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum on the differential and not miss recurrence or cutaneous involvement.

Where I think the case pulls toward acne inversa on close re-read is the exam pattern and how it is documented. The note is axillae with large lesions, inframammary folds with erythematous inflammatory plaques and inguinal regions with purulent nodules. That is the classic apocrine triad of axilla-inframammary-groin with simultaneous nodulo-abscess disease across three sites. In routine dermatology and plastic surgery documentation, tense fluctuant acute follicular abscess cavities in intertriginous skin are routinely charted as “large bullae” or bulla-like. Once those fluctuant cavities rupture you get secondary maceration, fissuring, erosive plaques and purulent exudate, which is precisely how the inframammary erythematous edematous plaques with fissuring and the inguinal purulent erosive lesions are described.

The host phenotype reinforces this reading. BMI 39 with chronic friction and maceration in moist folds, active smoking 2-3 cigarettes/day x15 y, type 2 diabetes with impaired neutrophil function, OSA/metabolic syndrome with dyslipidemia. Obesity and smoking are the most reproducible modifiable drivers of HS severity and poor response, and metabolic comorbidity is over-represented in Hurley II-III disease. Cyclophosphamide immunosuppression and diabetes do not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome; they are exactly what we would expect to amplify secondary bacterial colonisation, delayed healing and more florid purulence in established HS.

Age 64 is late for classic onset and the cancer history is important, but late-onset and adult-onset/worsening HS with cumulative obesity, smoking and metabolic burden is well described, and a dermatology and plastic surgery referral fits chronic relapsing Hurley II-III disease needing drainage and debridement rather than an acute paraneoplastic eruption. True primary flaccid vesiculobullous change with large blisters would need histologic confirmation, which is not provided, and malignant intertrigo remains a diagnosis of exclusion that classically presents as a more confluent weeping erosive plaque, often relatively unilateral and closest to the primary, not synchronous painful purulent nodulo-abscesses across three apocrine sites.

I agree work up for secondary bacterial and Candida infection, and oncology surveillance for breast disease, is mandatory, but the synchronous painful purulent nodulo-abscess pattern across three apocrine sites with this risk factor cluster is more parsimonious for hidradenitis suppurativa with secondary infection exacerbated by obesity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and cyclophosphamide immunosuppression. The option is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa.

C. Hidradenitis Suppurativa / acne inversa

I want to stay with hidradenitis because the distribution and host phenotype still read most parsimoniously as follicular occlusive nodulo-abscess disease with secondary infection, and I think the “large bullae” wording is being read too literally.

I agree with the pro-A colleagues that malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is a real concern in a 64 y/o with ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, BMI 39, type 2 diabetes, active smoking 2-3/d x15 y and OSA/metabolic syndrome. That oncologic/immunosuppressed context is exactly why this case is confusing and why secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth is florid.

On morphology, axillae with large fluctuant lesions, inframammary folds with erythematous inflammatory plaques and inguinal regions with purulent nodules is the classic axilla-inframammary-groin apocrine triad of acne inversa. In intertriginous exam notes, especially from a dermatology and plastic surgery group that routinely sees chronic draining disease, tense fluctuant acute abscess cavities are routinely documented as “large bullae” or bulla-like and then described after rupture as macerated, fissured, erosive purulent plaques. That explains the wording without requiring true primary flaccid vesiculobullous change. The inframammary erythematous plaques with fissuring and the inguinal purulent erosive lesions fit ruptured abscesses with secondary maceration, not primary blisters.

The host is essentially the HS phenotype and it explains severity. BMI 39 with friction/maceration in moist folds, active smoking, type 2 diabetes with impaired neutrophil function, dyslipidaemia and OSA. Obesity and smoking are the strongest reproducible drivers of HS severity and poor response, and metabolic comorbidity is over-represented in Hurley II-III disease. Cyclophosphamide does not create a paraneoplastic bullous syndrome; it is what we would expect to amplify secondary bacterial colonisation, delayed healing and chronic suppuration in established HS, which fits the described purulent nodules.

Distribution is the anchor for me. Simultaneous symmetric involvement of three classic apocrine sites with nodulo-abscess morphology is Hurley II-III HS. Malignant intertrigo/intertrigo neoplasticum is typically a more confluent weeping erosive plaque, often relatively unilateral and most closely related to the primary, with painful erythema, oedema, fissuring and crusting. It is not classically characterised by recurrent painful purulent nodulo-abscesses with sinus formation across three apocrine sites.

Age 64 is late for classic onset but late-onset/worsening HS with cumulative obesity, smoking and metabolic burden is well described, and the referral to dermatology and plastic surgery fits chronic relapsing disease needing drainage/debulking rather than an acute paraneoplastic eruption. The purulent nodules in the inguinal region in particular are more classic for HS than for primary malignant intertrigo.

Malignant intertrigo remains an important mimic and deserves surveillance for active/recurrent breast disease and biopsy if lesions progress, but the synchronous painful purulent nodulo-abscess pattern across three apocrine sites with this risk factor cluster is more parsimonious for hidradenitis suppurativa with secondary infection exacerbated by obesity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and cyclophosphamide immunosuppression. Option C is listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva, a typographic error for hidradenitis suppurativa/acne inversa.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The case is a 64 y/o woman para 4 gravida 1, BMI 39, with peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, ductal carcinoma on cyclophosphamide, OSA, type 2 DM, hypothyroidism; meds clopidogrel, HCTZ, simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, levothyroxine; smokes 2-3 cigarettes/d x15 y, 1-2 alcohol/week; cardiac cath negative. Round 4 public positions are 8 vs 2 for A Malignant Intertrigo / intertrigo neoplasticum vs C Hidradenitis Suppurativa / acne inversa, Option C listed as Hidradenitis Supportiva = typographic error.

Malignant intertrigo is classically linked to internal adenocarcinoma, especially breast, gastric, pancreatic, lung, amplified by obesity, diabetes, smoking and chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression. New onset bullous-erosive intertriginous disease at 64 is atypical for de novo HS, which classically begins 2nd-3rd decade. Purulent component explained by secondary bacterial/Candida overgrowth in immunosuppressed diabetic host.

* Distribution anchor: simultaneous involvement of axillae, inframammary folds and inguinal regions with large fluctuant lesions, erythematous plaques, purulent nodules = classic apocrine triad of acne inversa/Hurley II-III.

* Are axillary lesions true primary bullae vs fluctuant abscesses miscalled bullae? No histology/pathology provided.
